The Pine grosbeak Pinicola enucleator is a large, stocky finch of the subarctic and boreal forests, whose life history traits reflect the constraints of a harsh, seasonal environment. Eggs are incubated at 36 °C [T = 36 °C] and hatch after a period of approximately 13.25 days [ab = approximately 13.25 days], a duration consistent with the relatively short incubation periods observed in other cardueline finches that nest in cold climates. The newly hatched nestlings, weighing only about 4.3 grams [Ww0 = about 4.3 grams] at emergence, are altricial and entirely dependent on parental provisioning for both warmth and food. This low initial wet weight represents a minimal energetic investment per offspring at the point of hatching, a strategy that allows the female to channel resources into a relatively large clutch despite the brevity of the high-latitude growing season. The rapid transition from a yolk-dependent embryo to an exotrophic nestling is critical for maximizing reproductive output within a constrained temporal window.

Attaining an ultimate adult body mass of approximately 56.4 grams [Wwi = approximately 56.4 grams] requires a sustained period of rapid mass gain during the nestling and juvenile stages. This asymptotic wet weight, which is among the highest recorded for the genus Pinicola, is associated with a robust, thick-set body plan adapted for seed-cracking and cold tolerance. The energetic demands of reaching such a size are particularly acute during the nestling phase, when the developing chick must more than decuple its hatching mass over a short interval. Field records indicate that the time since birth at fledging, when the young bird first achieves sustained flight and departs the nest, is approximately 20 days [tx = approximately 20 days] under typical summer thermal conditions of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This fledging period of 16 to 20 days is comparable to that of other boreal finches and appears to be constrained by the rate of feather growth and the development of flight musculature.

Following fledging, young Pine grosbeaks enter a period of post-fledging dispersal and continued somatic growth before reaching reproductive maturity. Under the same active thermal regime of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], the time since birth at puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal activity, is about 60 days [tp = about 60 days]. This rapid maturation, occurring within a single summer, is an adaptation to the brief boreal summer, allowing birds hatched early in the season to potentially breed the following spring. However, the first successful reproduction event is typically deferred until the individual is a year old, with the time since birth at first brood estimated at 365 days [tR = 365 days] at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay between physiological puberty and effective first breeding is common among resident northern finches and is likely related to the challenges of securing a breeding territory and acquiring sufficient body condition to initiate a clutch.

Reproductive output in Pine grosbeaks is modest but consistent with a slow life-history strategy for a bird of its body size. Females typically lay 4 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 eggs per clutch] and raise a single brood each year [F_R_i = single brood each year]. The combination of a moderate clutch size and a low annual fecundity of a single brood is typical of species that invest heavily in parental care over an extended nesting cycle. The maximum reproductive rate is thereby constrained by the short window of food abundance in the boreal zone, during which adults must not only incubate and provision young but also replenish their own depleted fat reserves before winter. The thermal environment during the breeding season, averaging 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] for active adults, dictates the energetic costs of these activities, from foraging to brooding.

Maximum longevity in the Pine grosbeak has been documented to reach about 9.8 years [am = about 9.8 years] under natural conditions, a lifespan that is surprisingly long for a passerine of 56.4 grams [Wwi = 56.4 grams] and reflects the slow pace of life typical of high-latitude res at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]idents. This extended lifespan, recorded at an active body temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], allows individuals multiple breeding opportunities across their lives, a demographic trait that buffers against years of poor cone crop failure. In comparison to other finches of similar adult mass, such as the evening grosbeak, the Pine grosbeak exhibits a more pronounced longevity, possibly linked to its lower annual reproductive effort and its ability to exploit a stable, if periodically scarce, food supply of conifer seeds. The ultimate body mass of 56.4 grams [Wwi = 56.4 grams] is maintained through a diet that shifts seasonally from buds and berries in summer to conifer seeds in winter, requiring efficient energy storage and metabolic plasticity.
